newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allianz defends right to access Holocaust files.
newsitem.headline: Allianz defends right to access Holocaust files.

text.p: Allianz AG, one of 16 insurers embroiled in a legal tussle over missing Holocaust funds, on Thursday defended its right to access government files which plaintiffs say they have not been allowed to see.

Attorneys for Holocaust victims and their families allege that the German Restitution Office granted Allianz special government permission to research privileged and confidential files related to Holocaust victims.
In a statement issued from New York on Wednesday, the plaintiffs demanded that the insurance company should be denied this access to information.
Allianz, responding to an enquiry, confirmed that it had access to government files but said this was designed to aid claimants, not put plaintiffs at a disadvantage.
"We are very happy to have this access as it helps us to help people," a spokesman for the Munich-based insurance giant said.
The company needed access to state files to follow up cases which would otherwise have had to be dropped because of gaps in its own records, the spokesman said.
Moreover, German data protection laws clearly stated that both the insured party and the insurer were entitled to access insurance deeds, he said.
He conceded, however, that it might be easier for a company to gain access to deeds than it would be for an individual.
Allianz is one of 16 insurers named in a complaint filed earlier this year by Holocaust victims and their families which says insurers cheated Nazi victims of billions of dollars.
The suit claims that insurance policies held by the victims and their families were confiscated by the Nazis and then improperly transferred, liquidated or cashed in.
Allianz, while insisting that the bulk of claims against it have already been settled, has pledged to honour all reasonable outstanding claims.
The company is running a 24-hour hotline which descendents of victims of Nazi persecution can use to register their claims against the company.
But researching cases has proved difficult, not least because Allianz's files are sorted according to insurance number, not by name.
Allianz said it had requested further information from the German Restitution Office on between 600 and 900 claims, out of a total of some 1,200 claims being followed up.
Michael Witti, the plaintiffs' German co-counsel in the class action, is holding a news conference in Munich to protest about the situation on information.

Witti said in a statement that his request to review the government files had been denied unless the plaintiffs present original power of attorney and inheritance papers -- the condition waived for the Allianz defendants.
